title: Steinsaltz Opens the Talmud
hookLine: Rabbi Adin Steinsaltz translated and explained the Talmud for millions
carry: torah is everyone's, learned with a partner
tomorrow: what language did a grandmother pray in, if Hebrew wasn't hers?

cards: A family recipe that exists only in your great-grandmother's handwriting, in a language you can't read. You have it, and you don't.

For a long time the Talmud was like that for anyone without years of training: giant pages in Aramaic, no punctuation, arguments that start in the middle. Rabbi Adin Steinsaltz spent his life opening it.
He translated the Talmud into modern Hebrew, added vowels and punctuation, and explained each line in the margin, so a beginner could follow the argument. Not everyone cheered.

teach.b: Here are the two views, each in its own words. The first says: open it. The Torah was never meant for a few.
Deuteronomy calls it "an inheritance of the congregation of Jacob," all of it, for everyone. A book nobody can read teaches nobody.
If a nurse, a teenager or a retired pharmacist can sit down with a page and follow the argument, that is learning, and Steinsaltz made it possible for beginners to try. The second view says: careful.
The Talmud was built to be wrestled with, out loud, with a partner, a chavruta, and a teacher.
Pirkei Avot says, make for yourself a teacher, and acquire for yourself a friend.
The struggle over a hard line is where the learning happens.
An explanation printed in the margin can answer the question before you've even felt it, and a reader may finish the page without ever having been lost, or found.
Some teachers worried that the easy page would replace the hard room.

teach.h: THE SAME GOAL, A DIFFERENT DOOR.
teach.b: Notice that each side wants the same thing: people really learning. They differ about the door. One says the door was locked, so open it.
The other says the door is the wrestling, so don't skip it. And some learners do both: they open the translated page, then sit down with a partner and argue over it anyway.

how: Talmud is traditionally studied with a chavruta, a study partner, reading aloud and arguing line by line; the Steinsaltz edition, with its translation and notes, sits on study-hall shelves beside the traditional pages.

o: make hard learning reachable, then still wrestle with it
read sacred books only in their original languages
start any book from its very first page in order

games.q: two views on the open page — tap the pairs.
p: a study partner to wrestle with

s: the Talmud is written in plain Hebrew with modern punctuation
the traditional pages are largely Aramaic, without punctuation. Steinsaltz added vowels, punctuation and explanation.
the worry about easy translations was about skipping the wrestling
the second view says the struggle with a partner and a teacher is where the learning happens.
the two sides wanted different things

games.q: you love the explained, translated page. now state the other side's worry at its strongest.
o: a ready answer in the margin can end the question before you've wrestled with it.
translations are always wrong, so a beginner learns the Talmud backwards.
the Talmud should stay with scholars, since ordinary people can't handle it.
games.why: the strongest form of the worry isn't snobbery: Pirkei Avot pairs learning with a teacher and a friend, and the struggle is where it sticks. both sides want people really learning.

practice: Think of something you understand that someone near you finds closed: a book, a recipe, a game's rules, a page of your tradition. Write them a short text that opens one door into it, one line they could start from.
Send it if it feels right, or keep it as a version for later.

wordCard.voice: Open the book: Steinsaltz's life's work, a Talmud a beginner can follow. Ask the other side what the wrestling gives you, too.
